verdicts.conflict: Whether automated scoring models expand access for underserved populations or primarily reinforce systemic exclusion.
verdicts.rationale: Both camps cite plausible mechanisms without conclusive proof. The accelerationist claim relies on federal data showing increased loan approvals in low-income tracts, while the safetyist claim points to theoretical feedback loops and verification hurdles. Neither side provides comprehensive post-deployment audit data that reconciles both trends.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Independent, longitudinal audits of lending portfolios across multiple institutions that track both approval rates and default outcomes for demographic cohorts over a five-year period.

verdicts.conflict: Whether mandatory human review and oversight mitigate systemic bias or merely protect incumbent gatekeepers at the expense of efficiency.
verdicts.rationale: This values conflict weighs legal accountability against market speed. Accelerationists correctly identify that human reviewers exhibit documented cognitive biases, but safetyists accurately note that unverified software prevents legal recourse. Neither position accounts for hybrid models that pair automated scoring with structured human appeals.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical studies comparing error rates and demographic parity between purely automated decisions, purely human decisions, and structured human-in-the-loop workflows.
